title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: Arabic greetings are warm and formulaic. مرحبا and السلام عليكم are the essentials.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: السلام عليكم is the classic Islamic greeting; the reply is وعليكم السلام.
bullets: صباح الخير = good morning.
مساء الخير = good evening.
مع السلامة = goodbye.
تصبح على خير = good night.

steps.prompt: Match each Arabic greeting with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, how are you?":
steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · morning
steps.prompt: You hear this in the morning. What does it mean?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Peace be upon you, how are you?
steps.prompt: Return the greeting and answer warmly:
steps.explanation: "وعليكم السلام" is the expected reply to "السلام عليكم"; then "بخير شكراً. وأنت؟" answers and returns the question. "مع السلامة" is a goodbye.

steps.title: Check · hello
steps.prompt: Which is a standard hello?
steps.explanation: مرحبا is a common hello.

steps.title: Check · morning

steps.explanation: صباح الخير = good morning.

steps.title: Check · good night
steps.prompt: You’re heading to bed. You say…
steps.explanation: تصبح على خير is good night.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: Arabic interactions expect من فضلك and شكراً.

steps.title: Please & thanks
steps.body: من فضلك = please. شكراً = thank you.
bullets: شكراً جزيلاً = thank you very much.
عفواً = you’re welcome / excuse me.
آسف / آسفة = sorry.

steps.prompt: Match each Arabic polite phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A coffee, please.":
steps.explanation: Combining a request with "please" — the cornerstone of polite interaction.

steps.title: Listen · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says شكراً. A common reply is…

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Here you go, your coffee. Three riyals.
steps.prompt: Thank him as you pay:
steps.explanation: "شكراً جزيلاً" (thank you very much) is the natural response. "عفواً" is what the clerk would say back to you.

steps.title: Check · shop
steps.prompt: How do you say “please” when ordering?
steps.explanation: من فضلك is the standard please.

steps.title: Check · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says شكراً. A common reply is…
steps.explanation: عفواً means “you’re welcome.”

title: Numbers 1–10
description: Count clearly for prices, times, and quantities.

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: Arabic numbers have gender agreement in some forms. Start with the basic set.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: Numbers 1 and 2 agree with the noun; 3–10 reverse gender in classical style, but modern usage varies.
bullets: Learn the base forms first.
Practice with prices and ages.

steps.prompt: Match each Arabic number with its numeral:
Arrange the stones to say: "Two coffees, please.":
steps.explanation: Numbers in context — the essential combination for real-world transactions.

steps.title: Listen · age
steps.prompt: Someone says this. How old are they?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How many tickets do you want?
steps.prompt: Ask for two tickets:
steps.explanation: "تذكرتين من فضلك" uses the dual form for two tickets plus a polite please. "خمسة عشر ريالاً" is the price the clerk would quote.

steps.title: Check · seven
steps.prompt: What is “seven” in Arabic?
steps.explanation: سبعة is seven.

steps.title: Check · phrase
steps.prompt: “قهوتان” means…
steps.explanation: قهوتان = two coffees.

steps.title: Check · age
steps.prompt: How do Arabic speakers say “I am twenty years old”?
steps.explanation: عمري … سنة = my age is … years.

steps.body: A short self-introduction is enough: name, origin, and a polite close.

steps.body: تشرفنا (or سررت بلقائك) is a polite “nice to meet you.”

steps.body: Ask for "the bill" — servers rarely bring it unsolicited. Tipping customs vary by country.
bullets: For here or to go? — learn both forms.
A jug of tap water is often free — always worth asking.

title: Small talk & weather

title: At the restaurant
description: Ordering a meal and dietary needs.

steps.title: From table to bill
steps.body: Ordering follows a clear rhythm: being seated, choosing, ordering, and asking for the bill.

steps.title: Cultural notes
steps.body: Learn the word for the full menu vs. a set meal in your target language — they often differ.
bullets: Saying "Enjoy your meal!" before eating is polite in most cultures.
Dietary restrictions are best stated as early as possible.

steps.explanation: نباتية is the feminine form; نباتي is masculine.

title: Talking about plans
description: Express what you're going to do using the near future.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: Each language has a simple structure to talk about upcoming plans.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Learn the future or near-future structure for your language.
bullets: Portuguese: ir + infinitivo (vou visitar)
Arabic: س + verb (سأزور)
Hindi: future tense verb form (जाऊँगा)

phrases.source: What will you do this weekend?
I'm going to visit my parents.
We're going to watch a film.
She's going to travel to Cairo.

steps.prompt: Say you're going to visit your parents:

title: Telling time

title: Articles & gender
description: Noun gender and grammatical articles (or their equivalents).

steps.title: Nouns and their markers
steps.body: Portuguese has gender like French; Arabic has gender but a single definite article; Hindi has gender with no articles at all.

steps.title: Key differences
steps.body: Each language handles definiteness and gender differently.
bullets: Portuguese: o/a (the), um/uma (a) — 2 genders
Arabic: الـ (al-) for all definite nouns — 2 genders
Hindi: no articles; gender affects adjectives and verb agreement

steps.title: Check · to be
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am" in Arabic present tense?
steps.explanation: Arabic present tense drops the verb "to be" — أنا متعب (I tired) literally means "I am tired".

steps.title: Check · to have
steps.prompt: "لدي حجز" means…
steps.explanation: لدي = I have; حجز = reservation. Together: I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · idiom
steps.prompt: How do you say "they are hungry" in Arabic?
steps.explanation: جائعون is the masculine plural adjective for hungry. هم جائعون = They are hungry.

title: Regular verbs
description: Conjugate the most common verb family.

steps.title: The biggest group
steps.body: Most verbs follow a regular pattern — learn it once, apply it to hundreds of verbs.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Each language has its main verb conjugation pattern.
bullets: Portuguese: -ar verbs (falar) → falo, falas, fala, falamos, falam
Arabic: present tense uses prefix + suffix patterns: أتكلم، تتكلم، يتكلم
Hindi: verb + gender/number + tense marker: बोलता हूँ (m.), बोलती हूँ (f.)

steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · we form
steps.prompt: Which form is correct for "we speak"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you speak Arabic?
steps.prompt: Say yes, you speak a little Arabic:
steps.explanation: أتحدث (I speak) uses the أ- prefix for the first person singular present.

steps.title: Check · prefix
steps.prompt: What prefix marks the first person singular (I) in Arabic present tense?
steps.explanation: أـ marks the first person singular: أتكلم (I speak), أعمل (I work).

steps.title: Check · we form
steps.prompt: What prefix marks the "we" form in Arabic present tense?
steps.explanation: نـ marks the first person plural (we): نتكلم (we speak), نعمل (we work).

title: Adjective agreement
description: Make descriptive words match the noun they describe.

steps.title: Adjectives match their nouns
steps.body: Portuguese adjectives agree with gender/number. Arabic adjectives agree with gender, number, and definiteness. Hindi adjectives agree with gender and number.

steps.title: The default rule
steps.body: Add -a/-e for feminine in Portuguese; change the ending in Arabic; change -ā to -ī in Hindi.
bullets: Portuguese: alto → alta (f.), altos (m. pl.), altas (f. pl.)
Arabic: طويل (m.) → طويلة (f.)
Hindi: लंबा (m.) → लंबी (f.) → लंबे (m. pl.)

steps.prompt: Match each Arabic word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "She is tall.":
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · feminine
steps.prompt: Which adjective form goes with "أخت" (sister, feminine)?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: My brother is tall. And your sister?
steps.prompt: Describe your sister the same way:
steps.explanation: Arabic adjectives agree with gender: طويل (masc.) becomes طويلة (fem.).

steps.title: Check · feminine
steps.prompt: How do you say "she is short" in Arabic?
steps.explanation: هي is feminine → قصيرة (feminine adjective).

steps.title: Check · position
steps.prompt: Where do adjectives usually go in Arabic?
options: Always at the end of sentence
steps.explanation: Arabic adjectives follow the noun: مدينة جميلة (a beautiful city).

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with simple patterns.

steps.title: Negation patterns
steps.body: Each language has a characteristic way to negate a verb. Learn the pattern, apply it everywhere.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Position of the negative word differs.
bullets: Portuguese: não before the verb
Arabic: لا (present), لم + jussive (past), ليس (to be)
Hindi: नहीं after the predicate; मत for commands

steps.prompt: Match each Arabic word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I don't like coffee.":
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · لا
steps.prompt: Which is the correct negative form in Arabic present tense?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you like coffee?
steps.prompt: Say no, you don't like coffee:
steps.explanation: Arabic present-tense negation uses لا before the verb: لا أحب.

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: Where does لا go to negate a present-tense verb?
steps.explanation: لا goes directly before the present-tense verb: لا أحب، لا أعمل.

steps.title: Check · لم
steps.prompt: لم is used to negate…
steps.explanation: لم + jussive (apocopate) form negates the past: لم أذهب (I didn't go).

title: Asking questions
description: Question words and patterns.

steps.title: Asking around
steps.body: Each language has its own set of question words and question-formation patterns.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Yes/no and information questions each have their own structure.
bullets: Portuguese: rise in intonation + ? punctuation. Or verb-subject inversion.
Arabic: question word + normal word order. هل at start for yes/no.
Hindi: क्या at the start for yes/no; question words stay in the position of what they ask.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Arabic?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you have a question?
steps.prompt: Ask where she lives:
steps.explanation: أين تسكنين uses the feminine second-person (تسكنين) since Sara is female.

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Arabic?
steps.explanation: لماذا = why; it pairs with لأن (because) in the answer.

steps.title: Check · yes/no question
steps.prompt: Which word is used to form yes/no questions in Arabic?
steps.explanation: هل is placed at the start of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question.
